by.claim: displaced-work: the second thing going unstaffed is the stage-branch promoter, which the notes park as 'still the shell script, nobody owns it'. The hydrator RFC makes that component load-bearing by design: push-to-stage pushes hydrated manifests to a different branch and 'relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch', which is the RFC's declared integration point for automated environment promotion. T-26443 is that gap already firing — the stale-manifest auto-sync is observed only in push-to-stage mode, because the external promoter has not yet moved fresh manifests and auto-sync takes whatever the stage branch last held. An unowned shell script is the promotion system the RFC declined to build.

The PRD's 'Risks and Mitigations' section says 'No immediate Risks to consider', but the exact mechanism it proposes has already failed in staging before any of the money is spent: T-28511 reproduces an infinite delete/re-create loop on an ApplicationSet configured with a rollingSync step order and the reverse deletion strategy, where the wait-for-one-Application-to-be-fully-deleted step never completes because a child is stuck Progressing, and the controller restarts the wave from the top. The falsifying evidence for this bet is observable today, and the only thing standing between it and users is a runbook line telling operators to switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce before deleting any child by hand.

The roadmap records a standing commitment that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented and that teardown remains a manual operator action performed one Application at a time; the PRD's goal is exactly that feature, a `deletionOrder: Reverse` on `ApplicationSetStrategy` that deletes children in reverse of the `rollingSync` step order and waits for each to be fully deleted. Shipping the PRD does not extend the roadmap line, it reverses it, and nothing in the roadmap has been amended to say so.
